status: drafted by direct read of the real Geneva 1560 verse text (Assets/Resources/Verses/Geneva/amos_30.json, all 9 chapters/146 verses read in full), cross-checked against the existing validated KJV Amos.json for structural precedent only — not copied from it. Single-pass hand draft, not multi-agent workflow output.

characters.name: Amos

genealogy.note: No lineage given. Geneva 1:1 identifies him only as 'among the heardmen at Tecoa' (note the plural 'heardmen' and the Geneva spelling 'Tecoa', vs. KJV's singular collective 'herdmen of Tekoa'). He is dated 'in the dayes of Vzziah king of Iudah, and in the dayes of Ieroboam the sonne of Ioash King of Israel, two yeere before the earthquake.'

funFacts: Real Geneva-specific wording difference from KJV: at 7:14 Amos calls himself 'an herdman, and a gatherer of wilde figs' — Geneva says 'wilde figs' where KJV says 'sycomore fruit.' Read directly from the text, not assumed to match KJV's phrasing.

Twice personally turns aside a judgment God shows him in vision — the grasshoppers (7:1-3) and the fire that 'deuoured the great deepe' (7:4-6) — both times the text says 'the Lord repented for this.' No third such reversal follows; the later visions (7:7-9, 8:1-3, 9:1-4) go unanswered.

verses.note: Geneva superscription: 'The wordes of Amos, who was among the heardmen at Tecoa, which he sawe vpon Israel, in the dayes of Vzziah king of Iudah, and in the dayes of Ieroboam the sonne of Ioash King of Israel, two yeere before the earthquake.' Naming collision flag: 'Ieroboam the sonne of Ioash' is Jeroboam II, not the earlier Jeroboam I son of Nebat who founded Israel's rival worship system in 1 Kings — both share the bare name 'Ieroboam' elsewhere.
Opening theophany: 'The Lord shall roare from Zion, and vtter his voyce from Ierusalem, and the dwelling places of the shepheards shall perish, and the top of Carmel shall wither.'

First intercession: shown grasshoppers devouring 'the latter grouth after the Kings mowing,' Amos pleads 'O Lord God, spare, I beseeche thee: who shall raise vp Iaakob? for he is small.' Result: 'So the Lord repented for this. It shall not be, saith the Lord.'

Second intercession: shown the Lord calling 'to iudgement by fire' that 'deuoured the great deepe,' Amos pleads again in the same words. Result: 'So the Lord repented for this. This also shall not be, saith the Lord God.'

Answering Amaziah directly: 'I was no Prophet, neither was I a prophets sonne, but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of wilde figs. And the Lord tooke me as I followed the flocke, and the Lord said vnto me, Go, prophecie vnto my people Israel.'

Pronounces personal judgment on Amaziah's household after being told to stop prophesying: 'Thy wife shall be an harlot in the citie, and thy sonnes and thy daughters shall fall by the sworde, and thy land shall be deuided by line: and thou shalt die in a polluted land, and Israel shall surely go into captiuitie forth of his land.'

characters.name: Amaziah

genealogy.note: No individual family named. Amos's judgment oracle against him (7:17) mentions an unnamed wife 'an harlot in the citie' and unnamed sonnes and daughters who 'shall fall by the sworde' — none given personal names in the Geneva text.

funFacts: Called 'the Priest of Beth-el' (7:10) — Israel's royal state sanctuary under Jeroboam II, not the Jerusalem temple, making him a state religious official rather than an independent figure.
Calls Amos 'thou the Seer' (7:12) while ordering him out of Israel — an implicit acknowledgment of Amos's prophetic status even while trying to silence him.

verses.note: Reports Amos to the king: 'Amaziah the Priest of Beth-el sent to Ieroboam King of Israel, saying, Amos hath conspired against thee in the middes of the house of Israel: the lande is not able to beare all his wordes. For thus Amos saith, Ieroboam shall die by the sworde, and Israel shalbe led away captiue out of their owne land.'

Confronts Amos directly: 'O thou the Seer, goe, flee thou away into the land of Iudah, and there eate thy bread and prophecie there. But prophecie no more at Beth-el: for it is the Kings chappel, and it is the Kings court.'

Amos quotes Amaziah's own demand back before pronouncing judgment on him: 'thou sayest, Prophecie not against Israel, and speake nothing against the house of Izhak.' Naming note: 'house of Izhak' (Geneva spelling of Isaac) is a poetic name for the nation Israel here, not the patriarch Isaac of Genesis appearing in person.

characters.name: Oracles Against the Nations
characters.purpose: The Lord, through Amos, indicts eight nations in turn — Israel's neighbors and Judah first, then Israel itself — each with the identical refrain 'For three transgressions of ___, and for foure, I will not turne to it.' A rhetorical trap: a Judean/Israelite audience nods along condemning their enemies' war crimes, only to have the same formula land, unavoidably, on themselves at the climax (2:6-16).
funFacts: Real Geneva-specific naming difference from KJV: the Philistine city KJV calls 'Gaza' is rendered 'Azzah' throughout Geneva (1:6-8) — the same Hebrew place-name transliterated differently between translations.

Israel's own oracle (2:6-16) is by far the longest of the eight and the only one detailing covenant/social sins rather than war atrocities against foreign peoples — the true target the other seven were building toward.

verses.note: Damascus: 'For three transgressions of Damascus, and for foure I will not turne to it, because they haue threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of yron.' Fire sent into 'the house of Hazael,' devouring 'the palaces of Ben-hadad'; the people of Aram exiled 'vnto Kir.'

Azzah (Geneva's rendering of Gaza) and the Philistines: judged 'because they caried away prisoners the whole captiuitie to shut them vp in Edom.' Fire threatened also on Ashdod and Ashkelon: 'the remnant of the Philistims shall perish, sayth the Lord God.'
Tyrus: judged 'because they shut the whole captiuitie in Edom, and haue not remembred the brotherly couenant.'
Edom: judged 'because hee did pursue his brother with the sworde, and did cast off all pitie, and his anger spoyled him euermore, and his wrath watched him alway.'
The children of Ammon: judged 'because they haue ript vp the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border.'
Moab: judged 'because it burnt the bones of the King of Edom into lime.'
Iudah: judged 'because they haue cast away the Lawe of the Lord, and haue not kept his commandementes, and their lies caused them to erre after the which their fathers haue walked.'

Israel: the climactic, longest oracle — 'because they solde the righteous for siluer and the poore for shooes' — extended with real historical grievance ('I raysed vp of your sonnes for Prophets, and of your yong men for Nazarites... But ye gaue the Nazarites wine to drinke') and a closing image of even the mighty and swift unable to escape in that day.

characters.name: Social Injustice & False Worship
characters.purpose: Amos spells out exactly why judgment falls on Israel across chapters 3-6: exploitation of the poor, corrupt courts, luxury indifferent to national affliction, and hollow ritual worship offered without justice behind it — summarized in the book's own words, 'let iudgement runne downe as waters, and righteousnesse as a mightie riuer' (5:24).
funFacts: Real Geneva-specific wording difference from KJV: 5:24 reads 'righteousnesse as a mightie riuer' where KJV famously says 'as a mighty stream' — a genuine translation-choice difference in one of the book's most quoted lines.
'Kine of Bashan' (4:1) compares Samaria's wealthy, complacent women to the fattened cattle of Bashan's rich pastureland — one of the most pointed insults in the prophets.

verses.note: 'You onely haue I knowen of all the families of the earth: therefore I will visite you for all your iniquities' — election creates accountability, not exemption.
'Heare this worde, ye kine of Bashan that are in the mountaine of Samaria, which oppresse the poore, and destroy the needie, and they say to their masters, Bring, and let vs drinke.'
A refrain repeated five times across famine, drought, blight, pestilence, and overthrow 'as God ouerthrew Sodom and Gomorah': 'yet haue ye not returned vnto me, saith the Lord.'
Closing warning of the chapter: 'prepare to meete thy God, O Israel.'
'They afflict the iust, they take rewards, and they oppresse the poore in ye gate' — corrupt courts named directly.
'Woe vnto you, that desire the day of the Lord... the day of the Lord is darkenes and not light' — the expected day of vindication reversed into a day of judgment.

'I hate and abhorre your feast dayes, and I wil not smell in your solemne assemblies... but let iudgement runne downe as waters, and righteousnesse as a mightie riuer' — ritual worship rejected without justice behind it.
Those who 'lie vpon beddes of yuorie... but no man is sory for the affliction of Ioseph' — luxury indicted for its indifference, not the luxury itself.

characters.name: Visions of Judgment
characters.purpose: Where the first two visions of the cycle (grasshoppers, fire — covered under Amos himself) were turned aside by his intercession, these three are not: the plumbline/line vision, the basket of summer fruit, and the Lord standing beside the altar. Judgment moves from a warning that could still be averted to a sentence declared final: 'I wil passe by them no more.'
funFacts: Real, notable Geneva-specific content difference from KJV: the famous 'plumbline' vision (7:7-9) never uses that word in this translation. Geneva reads only 'a wall made by line with a line in his hand' and 'I wil set a line in the middes of my people Israel' — the word 'plumbline' (which gives the vision its usual name in English) simply is not present in this text.

9:6's description of God — 'He buildeth his spheres in the heauen, and hath laide the foundation of his globe of elements in the earth' — uses distinctly cosmological/astronomical language not found in this form in KJV's parallel verse, worth noting as a real Geneva-specific phrasing choice.

9:7 compares Israel to 'the Ethiopians' ('Are ye not as the Ethiopians vnto mee, O children of Israel, sayeth the Lord?') — a real textual reference relevant to this project's separate Ethiopian Bible indexing work, not an invented connection.

verses.note: 'The Lord stoode vpon a wall made by line with a line in his hand... Beholde, I wil set a line in the middes of my people Israel, and wil passe by them no more.' The hye places of Izhak (poetic name for Israel, Geneva spelling of Isaac) shalbe desolate; the Lord rises against 'the house of Ieroboam' (Jeroboam II, per 1:1 — not Jeroboam I of 1 Kings) 'with the sworde.'
Basket of summer fruit vision: 'The ende is come vpon my people of Israel, I wil passe by them no more... the songs of the Temple shalbe howlings in that day.'
Within the same vision unit: indictment of dishonest trade — making 'the Ephah small, and the shekel great,' falsifying weights, so 'we may buy the poore for siluer, and the needie for shooes.'

Vision of the Lord standing on the altar, commanding the lintel struck so the posts shake — 'he that fleeth of them, shall not flee away' — no intercession follows, unlike the first two visions. Closes with the doxology at 9:6: 'He buildeth his spheres in the heauen, and hath laide the foundation of his globe of elements in the earth: hee calleth the waters of the sea, and powreth them out vpon the open earth: the Lord is his Name.'

'Are ye not as the Ethiopians vnto mee, O children of Israel... haue not I brought vp Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistims from Caphtor, and Aram from Kir?' — Israel's election put in context alongside other peoples' own histories of deliverance, immediately before 'I will destroy it cleane out of the earth. Neuerthelesse I will not vtterly destroy the house of Iaakob.'

characters.name: Restoration of David's Fallen Booth
characters.purpose: After nine chapters of near-unrelieved judgment, the book ends on a sudden reversal: a promise to raise up the fallen tabernacle (booth) of David, rebuild ruined cities, and restore agricultural abundance — the book that opened with the Lord roaring in judgment (1:2) closes with unconditional hope.
funFacts: This passage is quoted directly by James at the Jerusalem council in Acts 15:16-17 as scriptural warrant for including Gentiles in the church — one of the most consequential New Testament citations of any Minor Prophet.

verses.note: Transition into the closing promise: 'I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corne is sifted in a sieue: yet shall not the least stone fall vpon the earth' — judgment on 'all the sinners of my people' but not annihilation of the whole.

'In that day will I raise vp the tabernacle of Dauid, that is fallen downe, and close vp the breaches therof, and I will rayse vp his ruines, and I will builde it, as in the dayes of olde... that they may possesse the remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen, because my Name is called vpon them.' Naming note: 'Dauid' here is a dynastic reference to the fallen Davidic royal line, not the person of David appearing on-page.

'The plowman shall touche the mower, and the treader of grapes him that soweth seede: and the mountaines shall drop sweete wine, and all the hilles shall melt... they shall no more bee pulled vp againe out of their lande, which I haue giuen them, sayeth the Lord thy God.'

genealogyLists.note: Bulk/unresolved references, kept out of the character list above — figures who are only chronological/reported markers and never speak or act on-page in Amos, matching the KJV Amos.json's own precedent of not giving them full character entries.

uzziah_geneva.note: 'Vzziah king of Iudah' — dating marker only, never appears in the narrative. Geneva spells the name 'Vzziah'; note the same king is called 'Azariah' through most of 2 Kings — one man, two names, not two kings.

jeroboam_ii_geneva.note: 'Ieroboam the sonne of Ioash King of Israel' — Jeroboam II, mentioned as the reigning king and reported to by Amaziah, but never speaks or acts directly in the book. Naming collision flag: distinct from Jeroboam I son of Nebat (1 Kings 11-14), who founded Israel's rival worship system generations earlier — both share the bare name 'Ieroboam' elsewhere in Kings/Chronicles.

notes: Geneva's Amos (146 verses across 9 chapters, matching the given canonicalOrder/verse-count) is structurally identical to the standard canonical Amos — no deuterocanonical or restructured content of the kind found elsewhere in this project's Ethiopian-translation work. The same 6-tier shape used for the validated KJV Amos.json was reused here (2 person-tier managers: Amos, and Amaziah promoted from background figure to full manager per rule 3 since he has his own confrontation scene, quoted dialogue, and a personally-named judgment oracle; 4 law/theme tiers covering Oracles Against the Nations ch.1-2, Social Injustice & False Worship ch.3-6, Visions of Judgment [the three unaverted visions, distinct from the two averted ones under Amos himself], and Restoration of David's Fallen Booth 9:11-15) — but every verse quote and every fact claim here was drawn fresh from the actual Geneva 1560 text, not copied from the KJV file. Real, notable Geneva-specific translation differences found and flagged in situ rather than silently normalized to match KJV expectations: (1) Amos calls himself a 'gatherer of wilde figs' at 7:14, where KJV says 'gatherer of sycomore fruit'; (2) the Philistine city KJV calls 'Gaza' is rendered 'Azzah' throughout 1:6-8; (3) 5:24's famous line reads 'righteousnesse as a mightie riuer' where KJV has 'as a mighty stream'; (4) most notably, the vision traditionally called 'the plumbline vision' (7:7-9) never actually contains the word 'plumbline' in this translation — Geneva says only 'a wall made by line with a line in his hand,' a genuine textual absence, not an omission in this draft; (5) 9:6's doxology uses distinctly cosmological phrasing ('spheres in the heauen,' 'his globe of elements in the earth') not matching KJV's parallel wording. Naming collisions flagged at every occurrence per the standing rule: Vzziah/Azariah (same king, two names, Geneva's own spelling of the KJV 'Uzziah'); Ieroboam (son of Joash, i.e. Jeroboam II) vs. the earlier Jeroboam I son of Nebat, flagged at both 1:1 and 7:9-11; 'house/hye places of Izhak' (7:9, 7:16, Geneva's spelling of Isaac) as a poetic name for the nation Israel rather than the patriarch appearing in person; 'tabernacle of Dauid' (9:11) as a dynastic reference rather than the person of David. All character/tier ids suffixed '_geneva' to avoid collision with the existing KJV CharacterIndex ids and any future Ethiopian-translation Amos entry. Geneva spelling preserved exactly in every direct quote (e.g. 'sayth'/'sayeth,' 'iudgement,' 'Iaakob,' 'Tecoa').
